A typical 1080p YouTube video might use **2–5 Mbps** (megabits per second), while Stadia’s own recommendations for 1080p gaming were **up to 20 Mbps** (and real-world usage often hovers around 10–20 Mbps). Here’s why that gap exists.

---

### 1. Real-time encoding vs. careful, offline compression
- **YouTube** can take hours or days to encode a video file. It uses the most advanced compression tools (like AV1, VP9, H.265), analyzes the entire video in advance, and carefully decides where to allocate bits. Long “Group of Pictures” structures allow it to send a full frame (I‑frame) only every few seconds, and then only tiny differences (P‑frames and B‑frames) for the rest. This is incredibly bandwidth‑efficient.
- **Stadia** has to encode each frame *as it is rendered*, with a delay measured in milliseconds. It can’t look far ahead, so it uses a much shorter GOP (often every frame or every few frames is a keyframe). The encoder must work fast, sacrificing some compression efficiency for speed. It simply can’t squeeze data as tightly as an offline encoder can.

### 2. Latency forbids large buffers
- When you watch a YouTube video, your device buffers several seconds (or even a minute) of video. If the network hiccups, the buffer hides it. This allows YouTube to use variable bitrate streaming (VBR) that dips to very low bitrates during simple scenes and spikes only when needed.
- Stadia cannot buffer. You need input-to-photon latency under ~80–100 ms, so the video stream must be sent almost instantaneously. To avoid stuttering or quality drops when the scene gets complex, Stadia must maintain a **consistently high bitrate** – you can’t afford a momentary dip that would cause a visible glitch. The result: constant high data usage instead of a variable, average‑low bitrate.

### 3. Game content is harder to compress
- Movies and YouTube videos are “natural” video: soft edges, motion blur, gradual changes. That compresses beautifully.
- Rendered games are full of sharp edges (UI elements, text, crisp textures), rapid camera movements, and explosions with high spatial detail. These are nightmares for inter‑frame compression, because tiny, high‑contrast details change drastically from frame to frame. Encoders have to spend more bits to avoid massive artifacts. So even with the same codec, a game scene at 1080p will inherently need a higher bitrate than a movie scene at that same visual quality.

### 4. Connection protocol and error handling
- YouTube uses reliable TCP (or QUIC) with retransmission, and it can wait for dropped packets. It can also preload multiple quality levels and switch seamlessly.
- Stadia streams over UDP (or WebRTC) for low latency. Dropped packets can’t be retransmitted without adding lag, so the stream must be robust against loss. Often that means padding the video with extra data (or forward error correction), and using a higher base bitrate to mask any corruption, further increasing usage.

That simply demands a much fatter data pipe than a pre‑recorded movie.
